appraisal_events.evidence: « Il était lui-même un homme intelligent, excédant les bornes de sa vie d'homme du monde... dans sa modestie de grand seigneur spirituel, eût lu en cachette les auteurs favoris de son fils pour apprécier de combien Saint-Loup lui était supérieur »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator imagines the late M. de Marsantes as intelligent and, in a gesture of modest generosity, secretly willing to recognize his son's intellectual superiority to himself; the reaction is explicitly hypothetical ('je crois bien que'), but the portrait itself is sincere, not ironized.

appraisal_events.evidence: « je vis qu'il ne nous saluait pas quoiqu'il ne pût ignorer que nous étions les amis de sa tante » ... « me tendit la main, à distance »
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup repeatedly fails to acknowledge the narrator and, when finally introduced, extends his hand at a deliberate distance, leaving the narrator feeling excluded; the passage itself later reframes this as impersonal family habit rather than targeted disdain, so the negative reading is unstable.

appraisal_events.evidence: « il ne me parla que de littérature, déclara après une longue causerie qu'il avait une envie extrême de me voir plusieurs heures chaque jour » ... « il m'avait témoigné une sympathie »
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup visits, converses warmly with the narrator, and expresses an intense wish to spend hours with him daily, reversing the earlier coldness and drawing the narrator into his favor.

ambiguities: The narrator's initial reading of Saint-Loup's failure to greet him as a personal snub is later explained in the same passage as an impersonal family habit rather than targeted disdain; the exclusion event (S2) is scored as the narrator's contemporaneous experience, but its ultimate meaning is destabilized by this later reframing.

status_effects.explanation: Marsantes is given a favorable, if speculative, portrait as intelligent and generously modest toward his son's superior mind.
The narrator registers repeated non-recognition and a distant, reluctant greeting from Saint-Loup as social exclusion, even though this reading is later complicated.
Saint-Loup's warm reception and stated desire for the narrator's company mark a clear local shift from exclusion to being sought out and included.
